question: to the Commission Elena Donazzan (ECR), Stefano Cavedagna (ECR), Carlo Ciccioli (ECR), Alessandro Ciriani (ECR), Daniele Polato (ECR), Mariateresa Vivaldini (ECR) Subject:

Electrolux’s 11 May announcement that it is planning to lay off 1 700 workers in Italy and close a plant in the country is, along with similar decisions made by Bosch and Beko, testament to the serious crisis that the European household appliances sector is currently experiencing. Europe used to be a leader in this sector, boasting as it did an integrated industrial ecosystem predicated on innovation, quality, research and a diversified and highly skilled production chain. The cold chain is of particular strategic importance, as it is crucial for food security, energy efficiency and quality of life. However, the competitiveness and attractiveness of low-cost production chains based outside the EU are progressively eroding European production capacity and know-how. The partnership that Electrolux has entered into with the Midea Group is also a concern, as this joint venture could result in the divestment of strategic assets, as has been the case in other areas of the green transition. In the light of the above: 1.

What will the Commission do to bring about a European industrial policy which specifically targets both the household appliances sector and the cold chain and aims to combat de-industrialisation and bolster the EU’s strategic autonomy?
Will the Commission strengthen certain EU instruments (state aid, investment screening) with a view to protecting Europe’s strategic production capacities?
How will the Commission go about supporting Member States, including the Italian Government, and ensure that goods are actually being produced in Europe?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthening Europe's industrial base and supporting the competitiveness, resilience and sustainability of European manufacturing industry, including energy-related products and their value chains. Through initiatives to boost innovation, skills, circularity and access to affordable clean energy, the Commission seeks to reinforce the EU's strategic autonomy. State aid tools provide many possibilities to support undertakings active in manufacturing. The Commission has expanded the possibilities for Member States to support certain strategic manufacturing capacities with the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework, helping European businesses meet the twin challenge of preserving competitiveness while advancing the clean transition for key strategic products. The revised EU framework for screening foreign investment further strengthens the EU's ability to address risks to security and public order linked to certain foreign investments, while preserving the EU's openness to investment. Furthermore, the Commission has proposed the Industrial Accelerator Act to boost industrial manufacturing capacities, notably in strategic sectors, through European preference and foreign investment conditions. As regards unfair competition from imports, the Commission acts to defend EU industry where it receives complaints with evidence that such imports are harming the industry in Europe. The Complaints Office of Trade Defence Services can be contacted to discuss the procedure1. To further equalize the level playing field between imports and EU-made products, the Commission proposed to extend the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism to downstream products in the steel and aluminium sectors.
